summary: Discusses principles for designing path signals, messages between applications and on-path network elements. Building on RFC 8558, it encourages authenticated signals with a minimal set of parties and calls for standards action in valuable cases.

plainLanguage.summary: Apps and the network between them sometimes need to pass notes. This says how to do that carefully and safely.

questions: how should applications talk to network elements
why is encryption important for path signals
subtitle: Design principles for explicit communication between apps and network elements

tldr.problem: Applications and network elements have evolved their interactions without comprehensive design, leading to unintended dependencies, protocol ossification, and information leakage.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides design principles for explicit path signals: intentional distribution, control of information, protection and authentication, minimization, limited impact, minimal entity sets, and careful mechanism selection.
tldr.outcome: These principles guide how endpoints and network elements should collaborate to improve network functions while protecting privacy and preventing misuse.

facts.label: Encryption effect
facts.value: Removes easy implicit signals, enables explicit design

today: RFC 9419 is an Informational document from the Internet Architecture Board published in July 2023, providing guidance for ongoing and future protocol design. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Unplanned Interactions
sections.content:
Applications and network elements have traditionally interacted in ad hoc ways, deriving information from visible data without explicit design. On-path elements examine TCP headers for latency and congestion; DNS names and TLS handshakes are monitored for purposes beyond their original intent; and features get repurposed in ways creators never imagined. This has caused several harmful effects: middleboxes have ossified TCP by creating dependencies on unmodified headers, creating perverse incentives against deploying better protocols; network behavior often relies on incomplete or incorrect information; and network entities expect to have rich visibility into sessions, encouraging pervasive monitoring.

Encryption is changing this landscape. QUIC protects end-to-end signals while still allowing explicit signals like the Spin Bit for latency measurements. This points to a path forward: intentional, authenticated, minimal-information collaboration can achieve network benefits without sacrificing privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: Apps and networks used to just guess what each other wanted by watching traffic. That caused problems: broken upgrades, sneaky spying, and too much information shared. Encryption lets us design better conversations.

sections.title: Design Principles for Path Signals
sections.content:
The RFC proposes seven principles for designing explicit path signal mechanisms.

Intentional distribution: Information should be provided knowingly and for a specific purpose, with no implicit signals leaking information accidentally. Each party should analyze the security and privacy implications of the information being shared.

Control of distribution: Senders must decide to send information to specific entities, and recipients must be able to agree or decline. All parties must be identified and potentially authenticated. Information directly relating to users should not be shared without user consent, prioritizing user interests over application developer interests.

Protecting information: Some information can exist in cleartext when not sensitive (like ECN bits), but in other cases secure signaling channels with authentication and integrity protection are necessary. Authentication does not equal trust.

Minimize information: Each party provides only what is needed for the task, applying this to information about applications, users, and networks. This includes how flows are identified.

Limiting impact: Path signals must have limited impact, scoped to specific network paths. Advisory information should not cause wide-reaching changes to multipath connections. The level of trust established determines the weight given to signals.

Minimum entity set: Designs should identify the minimum number of entities needed to share a signal. Even in closed networks, each interaction should be considered separately.

Carrying information: There is a distinction between what information is sent and how. Mechanisms should be designed to support specific minimal information sets rather than fully generic approaches that might enable mandatory information sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven rules: tell when you're talking, let people say yes or no, keep secrets, share only what's needed, don't let messages go too far, use the fewest people, and build specific tools not generic ones.

sections.title: Examples and Research Directions
sections.content:
The RFC notes that many existing functions fall short of these principles. For instance, using TLS SNI or DNS names for filtering reveals application identity without explicit consent. The document acknowledges open research challenges: securing communication with path elements is difficult from both mechanics and scalability perspectives; reducing effects of denial-of-service attacks without enabling censorship remains unsolved; protecting user information from widespread collection by servers and infrastructure requires new mechanisms; deploying network-to-application signaling has seen limited success; and data privacy regimes must address storage duration and purpose limitations.

Real examples show the tension: ECN bits are successfully shared for congestion information without privacy concerns, but proposals for quality-of-service mechanisms face business arrangement challenges. VPNs demonstrate explicit trust and coordination between applications and network elements, but finding practical, scalable trust mechanisms for other cases remains difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: Many things we try don't follow the rules. Some work: telling routers about congestion is fine. Others are hard: figuring out who to trust, stopping attacks without blocking good traffic, and keeping networks from spying on users.

sections.title: A Mindset Change for Network Collaboration
sections.content:
The RFC calls for a fundamental shift in how the Internet community approaches application-network collaboration. Rather than implicit signals that accidentally leak information, protocols should use explicit, designed, authenticated mechanisms that respect privacy and user interests. Future standards work in the IETF must focus on providing better alternatives and mechanisms for collaboration where it is beneficial.

This applies equally to information from applications to networks (application priorities, requirements) and networks to applications (congestion status, available bandwidth). Encryption enables this shift by removing the easy ability to use implicit signals and creating an opportunity to think through collaboration more carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: Going forward, engineers should design what apps and networks need to say to each other, rather than hoping they can guess from watching. Encryption makes it possible to keep it private while still being helpful.
